passage:
On the mud floor of Dadi's house in the village, Tushar stacked steel tumblers. One, two, three, crash. He whimpered and tried again. Crash.
Dadi reached over and held the bottom tumbler steady with one finger. Tushar stacked three, four, five.
"Me did!" he shouted, clapping.
His cousin Anirban laughed. "Dadi helped!"
Dadi winked at Anirban and put a finger to her lips. Tushar kept clapping.

qa.q: What was Tushar stacking?
qa.a: Steel tumblers.

qa.q: How does Tushar feel when the stack reaches five?
qa.a: He feels proud and delighted, shouting "Me did!" and clapping as if the win were all his own.

qa.q: What was helpful about Dadi's small touch?
qa.a: She steadied only the bottom tumbler with one finger, just enough for Tushar to do the stacking himself.

qa.q: Why might Anirban react differently to the tower?
qa.a: Anirban notices that Dadi helped, so to him it is not only Tushar's win, until Dadi signals to let Tushar enjoy it.

grounding: A toddler stacks tumblers once his grandmother steadies the base, and beams as if the win were all his own.

subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
subtype: Wanting a hint, not the answer [Actor]
passage:
The Pongal fair had given Harish a wooden bullock-cart puzzle, and by evening, under the verandah bulb, only four pieces were left. He turned one round and round. It wouldn't fit.
Madhuri Akka leaned over. "It goes..."
"Don't tell me!" Harish covered the puzzle with both arms.
"Okay, okay. Just a clue?"
He thought, then nodded, lips pressed together.
"Look at the wheel side," she said.
He frowned, turned the piece, and pushed. Click. "I did it! By myself!"
Madhuri grinned and said nothing about the clue.

qa.q: How many pieces were left by evening?
qa.a: Four pieces.

qa.q: Why does Harish cover the puzzle when Madhuri Akka starts to tell?
qa.a: He wants the win to be his own and feels protective of the puzzle, even though he is stuck and a bit confused.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri Akka's clue work well?
qa.a: It pointed him to the wheel side without giving the answer, so Harish could still fit the piece himself.

qa.q: What might Madhuri feel hearing "By myself!"?
qa.a: Madhuri likely feels amused and fond, happy to let Harish own the win.

grounding: A child stuck on a puzzle refuses the answer but accepts a small clue, then claims the win as his own.

subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
subtype: Help that is too much or too little [Receiver]
passage:
The winter-holiday maths camp at the community centre ran from nine to twelve, heaters humming. Kalyani stared at the word problem about two trains. Before she could underline anything, Sir leaned over, wrote the full solution in her notebook in neat red steps, and moved on.
"Got it?" he called back.
"Yes, Sir," Kalyani said. She hadn't. She copied it neatly and felt quietly small, like a guest in her own notebook.
Across the table, Indu had been given the Olympiad sheet with no help at all. After ten minutes she pushed it away and drew flowers in the margin.
Then the helper didi came by and asked Kalyani, "What do you know about the first train?" For the first time that morning, Kalyani picked up her pencil.

qa.q: What did Sir write in Kalyani's notebook?
qa.a: The full solution, in neat red steps.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel after copying the solution?
qa.a: She felt quietly small, like a guest in her own notebook, because she hadn't understood it.

qa.q: What kind of help finally got Kalyani working, and why?
qa.a: The helper didi's question, "What do you know about the first train?", which gave her a starting point without doing the thinking for her.

qa.q: What was the morning like for Indu?
qa.a: Indu, handed a sheet far beyond reach with no help, gave up after ten minutes and drew flowers in the margin, probably feeling defeated.

grounding: A student handed a full solution learns nothing while another left alone gives up, until a guiding question helps.

subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
passage:
Last summer I taught my little brother Darshan to cycle to the market on his own, and the hardest part was not the teaching. It was stopping. The first week I jogged beside him, hand on the seat, calling "Brake! Look left!" every few seconds. By the second week I noticed he was braking before I said it, checking the corner by the temple on his own. My hand hovered but didn't touch.
So one Saturday I stayed at the gate and just waved. My stomach was in knots the whole twelve minutes. He came back with the curd packet swinging from the handlebar, shouting, "Arohi Didi, did you see?" and grinning like he had conquered a mountain. I knew I had timed it right. Too early and he'd have wobbled into the gutter. Too late and he'd never have believed he could.

qa.q: How long was Darshan gone on the first solo ride?
qa.a: Twelve minutes.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel waiting at the gate?
qa.a: Arohi felt anxious, stomach in knots for the whole twelve minutes, yet trusted that stepping back was right.

qa.q: What signs told Arohi it was time to step back?
qa.a: Darshan was braking before being told and checking the corner by the temple on his own, needing fewer prompts.

qa.q: How did the solo ride feel for Darshan?
qa.a: Darshan felt triumphant, grinning like he had conquered a mountain as he came back with the curd packet.

grounding: An older sister notices her brother needs fewer prompts and steps back on purpose to let him cycle alone.

subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
subtype: Asking a mentor at the edge of competence [Response]
passage: Jasleen, you asked how I survived my first year in the lab. I was twenty-one, and Professor Rao handed me a project on soil bacteria. I knew nothing. My friends said, "Just nod in meetings and figure it out." Others said, "Wait, someone will show you." I did neither. I went to Meenakshi, the senior PhD student, and said, "I don't want you to do it. Can you show me how you'd plan it?" She drew four boxes on a napkin: question, method, control, record. I went away for two weeks and tried. I ruined three plates. Then I went back, and this time I asked, "Why does my control keep getting contaminated?" She smiled and said, "Now that's a real question, Deepak." That napkin is still in my drawer.

qa.q: What four boxes did Meenakshi draw on the napkin?
qa.a: Question, method, control, record.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel on first going to Meenakshi?
qa.a: Deepak felt out of depth but determined, wanting a way to think about the project rather than bluffing or waiting to be rescued.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Going back after two weeks and three ruined plates with a sharper question about contamination; trying alone first turned vague confusion into a real question.

qa.q: How might Meenakshi have seen Deepak's second visit?
qa.a: Meenakshi seemed pleased, smiling and calling it a real question, likely glad the framework had been used and not just asked for.

grounding: An elder recalls asking a senior for a framework on a first lab project, trying alone, and returning with sharper questions.

subtopic: Zone of proximal development and scaffolding
passage:
The client report was due at five, it was 4:20, and Gargi, three days into her first job, was stuck on the pivot table.
Pradeep rolled his chair over. His fingers itched for the keyboard; he could fix it in two minutes. He folded his hands instead.
"What have you tried so far?"
"I dragged region into rows, sales into values... and it shows the same total everywhere."
"Good. Check one thing: what's in the filter box?"
Gargi looked. Her face cleared. "Oh. Last month is still selected." She fixed it, then rebuilt the chart herself, slowly, tongue between her teeth.
At 4:52 she hit send. Pradeep's own work was now twenty minutes behind. He didn't mind. Next month she would be doing this without him.

qa.q: How many days had Gargi been in her first job?
qa.a: Three days.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling as his fingers itched for the keyboard?
qa.a: He felt impatient and tempted to take over, knowing he could fix it in two minutes, but chose to hold back.

qa.q: Which of Pradeep's coaching moves would you copy?
qa.a: Asking what she had already tried, giving one hint about the filter box, and letting her finish the chart herself, even under a deadline.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel after hitting send at 4:52?
qa.a: Gargi would likely feel relieved and more confident, having fixed it and rebuilt the chart herself.

grounding: A junior professional coaches a new hire with a question and one hint under deadline instead of taking over.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage:
At Noche Buena in Lola's crowded house in Quezon City, Tito Ben raised his glass. "Paulo! Ten years old already. What will you be?"
"An engineer," Paulo said at once, sitting up tall. "Like Papa and Lolo. The third engineer in the family."
Everyone clapped. Lola pinched his cheek. Paulo glowed.
Later, on the stairs with their plates of ham, his friend Siddiq from next door said, "I want to draw comics. Or maybe be a vet. I keep changing."
Paulo frowned. "You don't know yet?"
"Do you?"
"Of course," Paulo said. He had never once thought about it. It was simply true, like his name.

qa.q: What does Paulo say he will be?
qa.a: An engineer, like Papa and Lolo.

qa.q: How does Paulo feel when everyone claps?
qa.a: He feels proud and glowing, sure of his answer because the family expects it and nobody questions it.

qa.q: How could Paulo's family help him explore without taking away his pride?
qa.a: Ask what he enjoys and let him try different things, drawing, building, caring for animals, while saying any choice he makes later will be welcome.

qa.q: Why might Siddiq react differently to the question?
qa.a: Siddiq feels free to keep changing between comics and being a vet, perhaps because no single path has been handed over.

grounding: A child proudly announces he will be an engineer like his family, a role handed over rather than explored.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
subtype: Foreclosure under family or community pressure [Actor]
passage:
The Ramadan lanterns glowed in the window of the Berlin flat, and after iftar Rania filled in the summer internship form at the kitchen table. Workplace: Baba's pharmacy. Future plan: pharmacy degree. She had written the same words on every form since she was twelve.
That afternoon Felix had asked her in the school corridor, "If nobody expected anything, what would you choose?"
"Pharmacy, obviously," Rania had said, without a pause. "It's the family thing."
"But do you like it?"
She had shrugged. "It's decided. That's easier."
Now, pen in hand, she felt no excitement and no dread either. Just a flat grey feeling, like a room she had never really looked around. She signed the form and slid it across to Baba, who beamed.

qa.q: What workplace did Rania write on the internship form?
qa.a: Baba's pharmacy.

qa.q: What does Rania feel as she signs the form?
qa.a: She feels flat and grey, neither excited nor dreading it, like living in a room she never really looked around.

qa.q: What small step could Rania take to test the choice before committing?
qa.a: Spend a week somewhere different, a lab, a studio or a club, or talk honestly with Baba or a school counsellor about what she actually enjoys.

qa.q: How does Baba seem to see Rania's plan?
qa.a: Baba beams with pride, likely assuming her certainty means she truly wants the family path.

grounding: A teenager fills in the family-chosen career path with surface certainty and a quiet flatness underneath.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage:
Class teacher's note, Holi week, Class 9B. Sabina
Vijay has changed a lot since June. In term one he sat with the cricket boys and talked only scores. By August he was with the art-club group, nails painted black. Last month he was loudly arguing politics with the debate crowd; this week he sits alone at lunch. Today, at the Holi celebration, he refused colour, then later joined in, then snapped at a friend who asked which group he's with now.
He stayed back and said, "Ma'am, I don't know who I'm supposed to be." He looked genuinely unsettled.
I told him that trying things on is normal at his age and that he does not have to choose today. I will mention to his parents that he seems unsettled, and I have booked him a chat with the school counsellor next week, only to talk.

qa.q: Which group was Vijay with by August?
qa.a: The art-club group, nails painted black.

qa.q: What is Vijay feeling when he says "I don't know who I'm supposed to be"?
qa.a: He feels unsettled and confused, which also shows in snapping at a friend and sitting alone at lunch.

qa.q: What did the teacher do next, and why does it help?
qa.a: The teacher told him trying things on is normal, took away the pressure to choose, and arranged a counsellor chat and a word with his parents, so he has support while exploring.

qa.q: How might Vijay's friend feel when snapped at?
qa.a: The friend was likely hurt and puzzled, asking a simple question and getting an angry answer.

grounding: A teacher notes a teenager moving through friend groups and styles, unsettled about who he is, and arranges support.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage:
The college was half empty for the Puja break when Noor sat in the advising office, her third change-of-major form on the desk. Economics in first year, sociology the next semester, now media studies.
Tejas Sir, the advisor, didn't sigh. "Tell me what you've learned from all this switching."
Noor pulled out a battered notebook. "Economics: I hated the models but loved the village survey. Sociology: loved the interviews. The Spiti trip: I spent every evening recording the old women's stories. The photo club, the theatre club, the quiz club... only the stories stuck."
"So what's the pattern?"
Noor paused. "People's stories. Fieldwork. Maybe documentary."
"Good. You have until next semester to commit," he said. "Explore with that question now, not just more clubs."

qa.q: Which change-of-major form was on the desk?
qa.a: Noor's third change-of-major form.

qa.q: What might Noor be feeling as she names the pattern?
qa.a: She seems thoughtful and a little surprised, pausing before seeing that people's stories and fieldwork run through everything she enjoyed.

qa.q: What makes Noor's exploring useful rather than drifting?
qa.a: She kept a notebook reflecting on what she loved and hated in each try, so the switching produced a pattern she can build on.

qa.q: Why might Tejas Sir not sigh at a third form?
qa.a: Tejas Sir likely sees exploring as normal at this stage and cares more about what Noor has learned than the number of switches, while still setting a deadline.

grounding: A student who has switched majors and tried trips and clubs reflects with an advisor and finds a pattern to commit to.
